lines.text: אב 2 אב
أَبٌ, constr. أَبُو, أَبِى, أَبَا, Chald. and
Syr. אַבָּא, ܐܰܒܳܐ.
1. In a proper sense, Gen. 19, 31 sq.
44, 19. 20. al. sæpiss.—But the word
father often has a wider sense; see
Fesselii Adv. Sacra VI. 6. E. g.
2. i. q. forefather, ancestor, 1 K. 15, 11.
a great-grandfather, Num. 18, 1. 2. 1 K.
15, 11. 24. al. Is. 43, 27 אָבִיךָ הָרִאשׁוֹן חָטָא
collect. thy first forefathers sinned.—
Very frequent in Plur. אָבוֹת fathers,
i. e. forefathers, Gen. 15, 15. Ps. 45, 17.—
For the phrase נֶאֱסַף אֶל־אֲבוֹת, see un-
der אָסַף.
3. i. q. the founder, author, i. e. first
ancestor of a tribe or nation, Gen. 10, 21.
Here we may refer Gen. 4, 21 the fa-
ther of all such as handle the harp and
the pipe, i. e. the founder of the family
of musicians, the inventor of the art of
music.
4. Of the author or maker of any
thing, espec. a creator; Job 38, 28 hath
the rain a father? i. e. creator. In this
sense God is called the father of men,
their Creator, Is. 63, 16. 64, 7. Deut. 32,
6; comp. Jer. 2, 27.—Here too may be
referred Job 34, 36 אָבִי יִבָּחֵן אִיּוֹב, Vulg.
mi pater, probetur Jobus, i. e. my Father,
let Job be tried; but the sense is lan-
guid. Others not unaptly make אבי i. q.
אֲבוֹי wo!
The above tropical senses come from
the notion of source, origin; others are
drawn from the idea of paternal love and
care, the honour due to a father, etc. E. g.
5. i. q. a nursing-father, benefactor, as
doing good and providing for others in
the manner of a father. Job 29, 16 I was
a father to the poor. Ps. 68, 6 a father
to the fatherless. Is. 22, 21 a father to
the inhabitants of Jerusalem, spoken of
Eliakim the prefect of the palace. Is.
9, 5 אֲבִי עַד the everlasting father of his
people, i. e. the Messiah; comp. pater
patriæ among the Romans. By the
same metaphor God is called the father
of the righteous and of kings, and these
also are called his sons, 2 Sam. 7, 14.
6. For a master, teacher, from the idea
of paternal instruction, 1 Sam. 10, 12.
Hence priests and prophets, as teachers
sent with divine authority, are saluted
with the title of father, out of respect
and honour, even by kings, 2 K. 2, 12. 5,
be unto me a father and a priest. 18, 19.—
So the Rabbins are called אָבוֹת fathers;
much as we use the honorary appellation
of fathers of the church, the holy father
i. e. the pope.
7. Spec. father of the king, in a similar
sense, i. e. his chief adviser and prime
minister, whom the modern orientals call
Vizier. Gen. 45, 8 וַיְשִׂימֵנִי לְאָב לְפַרְעֹה
and hath made me a father to Pharaoh.
So Haman is said to be δεύτερος πατήρ
to Artaxerxes, Sept. Esth. 3, 13; comp.
1 Macc. 11, 32. Comp. also Turkish
اتابك Atâbek, father-prince, and Lala
father, spoken of the Vizier; see Ja-
blonsky Opusc. ed. te Water, T. I. p. 206.
Barhebræi Chron. Syr. p. 219. l. 15.—
Some of the ancient interpreters un-
derstand the same by the word אַבְרֵךְ
Gen. 41, 43; explaining it father of the
king, or of the land, kingdom; so Luther.
8. As expressing intimate relationship,
close alliance. Job 17, 14 לַשַּׁחַת קָרָאתִי
אָבִי אַתָּה to the grave I said, thou art
my father; and in the other hemistich,
to the worm, thou art my mother and
my sister; comp. Ps. 88, 19.
9. In Arab. and Ethiopic, the name
father is also put trop. for possessor, and
is spoken of one who excels in any thing,
and is distinguished for it, e. g. أبو شام
father of odours, i. e. an odoriferous tree.
So in Heb. only in pr. names, e. g.
אַבְשָׁלוֹם father of peace, i. e. pacific.
Note. The grammatical form of this
noun may be said to follow the analogy
of verbs ל״ה, as if for אָבֶה, Lehrg. § 118.
Still it is no doubt primitive; since
both אָב father and אֵם mother imitate
the simplest labial sounds of the infant;
as also πάπας (παππάζω), papa, pappus,
avus, Turk. بابا.—Besides the usual
form of the constr. אֲבִי there is also
an ancient form אַב, or also אֲב, (like יַד,
יֶדְכֶם,) found only in compound proper
names, as אַבְרָהָם, אַבְשָׁלוֹם, אֶבְיָתָר; al-
though even in these the form אֲבִי is also
often employed, as אֲבִימֶלֶךְ, אֲבִיעֶזֶר.

line_status.note: The only difference is the final letter of the third form: the print shows a dotless final yā (ى), with no two dots beneath it, as Reading A has; Reading B's dotted ي is not printed. Order (أَبُو, أَبِى, أَبَا), hamzas, fatha/damma/kasra and the tanwīn on أَبٌ all match both readings.

Only difference is spacing after the comma in the final reference: the print is set tight at line end with no visible space between "17," and "10", so Reading B matches; everything else (13. 6, 21. 13, 14. (comp. 8, 9.) Judg.) is identical in both and in the print.

The vowel under the aleph of אתה is a plain horizontal stroke (patach), with no descending tick below it that would make it a qamets; Reading B's אַתָּה matches the print (and the standard Job 17:14 pointing). Everything else — אָבִי, the dagesh in tav, and the English — is identical in both readings and matches the image.
The alif of ابو carries a printed hamza above it (أ), clearly visible as a mark over the tall stroke; Reading A omits it. Shin has its three dots; no other vowel marks are printed.
The Arabic بابا is printed without vowel points: only the subscript dots of the two bā' are visible, no fatḥa strokes above, so Reading B's بَابَا adds unprinted vocalisation.
Under the aleph of the second אב the print shows a hataf patah (two stacked dots beside a short horizontal stroke), not a qamets; Reading A's אָב is wrong, Reading B's אֲב matches the print.

Decisive difference is the vowel under the initial alef of the 2nd and 3rd names: the print shows a plain pataḥ (single horizontal stroke, no adjacent shewa dots) under א in אַבְשָׁלוֹם, and a segol (three dots) under א in אֶבְיָתָר — not ḥataf-pataḥ as in Reading B. Order of the three names, plene ו in שָׁלוֹם, shin dot, and all other points match Reading A.
